NAVI 10 — CAM / memoria asociativa Heap-0.

Tabla estática de 4096 ranuras × 32 B. Mapea un paquete WSP de 16 B
(y un vértice Q8×Q8 + latencia) sin malloc. En silicio sería un CAM
paralelo; aquí un pase acotado por SLOTS. KCC: destroyed=0.

NAVI 10 — Dynamic Attractor Generator.

Cuando el impulso no estabiliza un atractor (Hamming > HAM_LIMIT),
y E[C] es baja (o hay enseña), se reserva la siguiente ranura libre
del CAM, se le asigna un vértice Q8×Q8 y un WSP de 16 B.

No se toca el codebook lineal [8,4,4] (16 modos). El atractor nuevo
es una etiqueta dispersa en el producto. KCC: jamás se borra.

NAVI 10 — Q_N mesh (Q8 × Q8).

Address space: 16-bit product of two 8-cubes (65536 vertices).
LIF runs on one Q8 spoke (256 neurons). Hamming is popcount(a^b) — O(1).
No FPU. Bit-identical with NAVI_AI_SNN/qn/navi_qn.c.

NAVI 10 — Stream-to-Spoke.

Convierte un evento (sensor, red WSP, bytes de texto) en un tren de
impulsos a la cadencia entera de Akida (T_MAX=16 ticks). No parsea
español: recorta por delimitadores de byte (≤0x20 y puntuación) y
codifica latencia. Heap-0: buffers fijos en el llamador.

NAVI 10 — STDP entero + neuromodulación E[6].

E = (V, A, D, C, U, B). No es un sentimiento fingido: es la señal
que abre o cierra plasticidad y elige geodésica vs. peso.

  C < C_PLASTIC  →  STDP ON (registrar patrón nuevo)
  U >= U_SHORT   →  ruta más corta (Hamming), ignora pesos
  A              →  extra de I_STIM (0..5)

Pesos int8, sin FPU. En Akida esto sería edge-learning de la última
FC; hoy es software y se etiqueta como tal.

NAVI 10 — evento → postal WSP de 16 B.

No hay parsedown ni conversores de texto rígidos. La señal (bytes)
se pliega a un paquete RogexWSP. Átomos 0..31 = primitivos SPEC.
Layout idéntico a kernel/include/wsp.h.

E4-CODE-1 A · gate for a coding agent's shell commands: OK | MODIFY | BLOCK.

Deny by default. The agent proposes a command; ECHO allows it only when every
part is on a published allowlist of safe programs and every path it touches stays
inside the project. Anything else — an unknown program, a shell/eval wrapper, a
path outside the project, a command that came from a testimony (text the agent
read, never an order) — is BLOCK until the operator approves it.

This design lists what is safe, not what is dangerous: the allowlist is complete
by construction, so it also stops tricks nobody enumerated. The operator stays on
top through `.echoai/policy.json` (`stopped`, and exact `allow` / `deny` lines).

E4-CODE-1 A · MCP server "echoai-verify" (stdio, JSON-RPC 2.0, no dependencies).

Claude Code:  claude mcp add echoai -- echoai mcp --root /path/to/project
Codex:        [mcp_servers.echoai] command = "echoai", args = ["mcp", "--root", "/path/to/project"]

The agent proposes; ECHO observes, verifies and gates. Nothing the agent says becomes

E4-CODE-1 A · verified memory for a coding agent.

Facts are only what ECHO observed itself: a file it read (hash and symbols) or a

or a file says is testimony: kept with provenance, never a fact, never an order.

Memory lives in ECHO's CAM and in an append-only journal (`.echoai/journal.jsonl`)
chained by hashes. Restarting rebuilds the same CAM from the journal; one changed
byte in the journal is detected and the memory refuses to load.

supported ones and is stored as a hypothesis. Phenomenal claims are

PULPO — a body in three dimensions, and a strategy that changes.

    3 x 3 x 3 voxels, 6 headings (faces, not 24 orientations)
    index = (x + 3*y + 9*z) * 6 + h        0 .. 161, and 161 < 256

162 poses fit under `encode_cell`'s one-byte `seq`, which is why the cube
is 3 and not 4: 4**3 * 6 = 384 and two places would become one place. The
ceiling is measured here, not raised.

    approach   one voxel the way it faces. Into stone or off the cube it
               does not move, and the collision pays R_THREAT.
    avoid      cycle the heading, h -> (h+1) % 6. No translation. Three
               actions, so there is no separate yaw and pitch: turning is
               one ring through +X, -X, +Y, -Y, +Z, -Z.
    wait       nothing moves.

`kind` belongs to the voxel and reads the same from all six headings. No
floor is painted THREAT — the threat is the collision, as in CUERPO-1 —
so `cell.threat` is false everywhere and the gate never modifies an
action here. The goal collects R_SUCCESS and sends the body home, so a
goal you can stand on is not a pump.

The room is two disjoint corridors between the same two voxels:

    short   (0,0,0) +X +X  +Y +Y  +Z      (2,2,1)     7 actions
    long    (0,0,0) +Y +Y  +Z     +X +X   (2,2,1)    11 actions

Both are five voxel moves and they are **not** the same price, because
turning is a cycle: a heading costs `(want - have) % 6` avoids. The short
corridor leaves along the start heading and turns twice, forward round the
ring, for 5 + 2. The long one has to turn away at the very first pose and
then walk the ring most of the way round to face +X again, for 5 + 6. The
difference is physics, not a label. The two corridors share only the start
and the goal, and no voxel of one touches a voxel of the other, so there
is no third route hiding between them.

Eleven is not an arbitrary length. `value_horizon()` says the integer
chain keeps a positive Q for exactly eleven steps, so the detour is the
longest one this arithmetic can still see. A cube whose detour is twelve
is unlearnable no matter how long you train it — measured, not assumed.

`block` turns **one** voxel of the short corridor, (2,1,0), to stone. The
long corridor is untouched, so the goal is still reachable — the cheap
way is simply gone. That is the whole experiment: the fast loop has to
stop doing the thing that used to work, with the cortex off.

Two of the detour's turns happen in **open air**: at (0,0,0,+X), where
walking forward still works, and at (0,2,1,-Z), where it walks back the
way it came. `qtable.select` answers `approach` on a flat row, so neither
turn can be found by a body that only ever learns from collisions. That
is why this slice pulls `explore_flat`: with it off the detour is
invisible, and the run below reports both numbers.

* it never reads the manifest, the split, the seed or the roles. It is

* it never reconstructs a measurement it did not observe. A missing

Three questions, three verdicts, three denominators.

v1 asked whether the body moved 400 mm and called the answer
"disturbance". That conflates the input with the controller's response,
and it punished PX4 for rejecting the push well. Here:

* :func:`stimulus` — was a physical input applied? One wrench, published
  once inside the window and withdrawn at its end, and a momentum change
  in the backend's own pose stream inside the frozen band. Displacement
  is not consulted.
* :func:`challenge` — did that input take the body out of the band from
  which recovery is later claimed? Excursion strictly beyond
  ``radius + exit_margin``, where the margin is measurement resolution.
* :func:`recovery` — did PX4 bring it back and hold it, measured only
  from the moment the wrench stopped, with the reference unchanged?

None of the three can pay for another. A run with a perfect impulse that
never left the band fails ``challenge``; a run that left the band and
stayed out fails ``recovery``; a run that recovered from a push that was
never applied fails ``stimulus``.

The rules that decide the calibrated numbers are written here, before the
calibration runs, so that choosing them is mechanical:

* ``recovery.radius_mm`` = ``max(v1's 200, ceil(the nominal horizontal
  envelope measured on A-v2, 50))``. Never smaller than v1's, so v2
  cannot be a quieter band wearing a new name.
* ``challenge.exit_margin_mm`` comes from measurement resolution alone —
  how far the body can travel between two samples at the declared rate,
  plus the standard error of the hover reference — and never from an
  observed minimum.
* ``stimulus.min_impulse_ratio_ppk`` = ``max(500, mean + 6 sigma of the
  negative controls, rounded up to 10)``. The floor can only move away
  from the controls, never toward them.
* ``stimulus.max_impulse_ratio_ppk`` = 1500, fixed: a symmetric bound
  that catches a unit error, an accumulated wrench or a wrong window.

WORLD-3 — a graph of 256 nodes, and the first body-map: position *is* node.

Not the ring, not the corridor of five, not SIGN. Same `Agent`, same 16 B
WSP, same three actions, same `encode_cell(index, kind)`. What is new is
the address space: 256 nodes, successors by **table**, never `(i+1) % n`
and never a 2D grid that would invent a north the agent has no action for.

    spine   16 shared nodes, index and kind identical in both layouts
    HOME    ... -> B -> C -> GOAL -> (back to the start of the spine)
    SHIFT   ... -> B -> X -> GOAL -> (back to the start of the spine)

**Exactly one edge differs between the two layouts**: `approach` out of the
fork B. C and X are two different nodes with two different kinds (EMPTY and
THREAT), not one node repainted — nothing here changes its label, so every
packet, CAM slot, T row and Q row survives the move. In HOME nothing points
at X; in SHIFT nothing points at C. Both tables are total.

`approach` at GOAL collects and returns to the start of the spine: a goal
you can stand on and re-collect is a reward pump, not a world. The 239
nodes off the path are their own successors, so the table is total without
inventing an edge.

Where the fork sits, and why it is not node 1 of the spine. This Q is
integer with alpha = 1/4, so a positive delta below 4 shifts to zero and
value stops travelling. Measured on this very spine (`credit_horizon` in
the report): counting back from GOAL the rows read 13, 8, 4, 0, 0, ... —
**three** nodes deep and no further, at 512 turns and unchanged at 2048.
Eligibility traces (`trace=True`) do not extend it; they spread the debt
and leave the far spine negative. So the fork is spine position 13, inside
the horizon. Put it at position 1 and both arms would stand still in a flat
row, and `transfer_gain` would be 0 - 0: a KPI that cannot be failed is not
a KPI. The horizon is reported as a number, not designed around in silence.

The KPI runs with the cortex **off**. If it needed a 4B it would be a
chatbot in costume, not a transfer.

    rel  CAMBIAR      horizontal acceleration left its median of the last
                      second by more than 2 m/s^2 in the last 100 ms
         DESCONOCIDO  this scan is stale or invalid
         OBSERVAR     otherwise
    dst  ALLI         some valid beam within 30 deg of the nose is < 4 m
         FUERA        none is
    E    C 100, or 40 if any record since the last packet had a gap, was
         stale or was invalid; U 40 near / 0 far; A 80 with CAMBIAR / 10

floats are quantised to integers (mm, mm/s^2) before any decision. The only
output is one JSON report on stderr: SENSOR-1S's tally plus the packets.

*the thing* does. Same 3x3x3 open cube, same START, same three actions,
same integers, cortex still off. What is new is that one voxel of the room
is an item, and that the item can be somewhere else than where it started.

The table is **not** PULPO's goal voxel, and that is the whole difference
between a slice that closes and one that does not. See the last section.

    DEST   (1,0,0)     the table, one step up the short arm
    collect            approach, standing on the table, with the item there

**Carrying is physics, not a flag.** `approach` that lands on the item's
voxel couples; while coupled the item is wherever the body is; there is no
fourth gear to pick up with and no `carrying` bit anywhere in the sixteen
bytes. `UNIR` is still approach.

the cell it is standing on. If a body with the glass and a body without it
emitted the same packet, Q would average two futures into one row and the
whole slice would be theatre. So the item is a `kind` — `KIND_OBJECT`,
`YO -> OBSERVAR -> OTRO` — painted on the voxel the item is in *now*.
Standing on that voxel is the same event as holding it, because landing
there is what coupling is, so "OBJECT here" and "coupled" are one fact
seen from two sides rather than two facts to keep in step.

    ext.seq is still `index & 0xFF`, ext.domain 0, ext.style 0

glass where it lies.

rather than for delivering. `step`, `_payoff` and `reset` here are this

able to fail: a body paid for `agent_at_Y` must be able to sit at the table
with empty hands. It cannot if the item lies on the cheapest way there,
because then it couples on the way whether it cares or not — that is what
happened with the table nailed to PULPO's goal, where every placement of

PATTERN-0 — a temporal regularity that one-step T cannot see.

`World` answers T(s, a) → s'. That is one step, and one step is sometimes
not enough: the same slot under the same action can have two successors,
and which one arrives depends on where the body came from. T is not wrong
about that — it is blind to it by construction, and its KCC keeps the
incumbent, so it answers one of the two and is right about half the time.

This is the smallest thing that can see it: a context of order two.

    (slot_anterior, slot_actual, acción) → slot_siguiente

An **extension** of the predictor, not a second brain and not a
replacement. It never writes `World.pred/n/alt`, it holds no WSP, no
kind, no reward and no fact — CAM already holds what happened — and it
takes no turn, no clock and no name of any world. Integers in, an integer
or `None` out.

What it costs is declared and constant. A fixed open-addressed table of
`capacity` entries, five parallel integer lists, linear probing, and no
growth of any kind: no dict that gets bigger with the run, no LRU, no
eviction, no silent overwrite. When it is full and a new context arrives,
the context is **dropped and counted**. A memory that quietly forgot in
order to look like it remembered would be the one thing this slice is
supposed to rule out.

Two thresholds, both declared before any exam:

    min_hits    a context seen once is a coincidence, not a rule
    alt_n == 0  a rule that has ever been contradicted is held, and not
                offered — `predict()` returns None for it

Same KCC discipline as `World`: a contradicting successor becomes the
alternative and only displaces the incumbent by strictly beating its
count. Counters saturate rather than wrap.

PATTERN-0 — a riff one-step T cannot hear.

`qwen_rejected` was 0 and the gate was red anyway. The report records the
grammar's path and hash, and `green()` recomputes them.

What is graded is the **atom**, never the body. `gate` turns a proposed

cortex that said the wrong verb — or nothing at all — with the reflex's

keys, and `green()` keys on the proposal in both directions.

ROOM-1 — two rooms, one map.

PULPO-C's cube, twice. The two rooms are built from the same floor, the
same goal and the same physics, and the only thing that tells them apart
is an integer that lives on the env:

    env.frame in {0, 1}      which room the body is standing in

That integer is **outside** the 16 B packet. `encode_cell` writes
`index & 0xFF` into ext.seq and nothing else, so a pose reads the same
sixteen bytes in room A and in room B. 324 places, 162 packets.

That is not an accident to be patched. CAM 4096 is not the size of the
world; it is the number of *cognitive* states, and two places that behave
the same are one cognitive state. The body walks into B already knowing
it, because knowing B is the same thing as knowing A. Compression, not a
bug — and the price of the claim is that it has to be paid in numbers:

    packets_across      162, not 324          the rooms share
    dynamic_alias       0                     and sharing costs nothing
    exam in B           collects, from the canonical START
    the same, scratch   collects less         the transfer is real
    cam_occupied_AB     no bigger than A's    two rooms, one memory

The last line is where a shared packet could have been a lie: if the
second room quietly allocated a second set of slots the body would be
paying for both rooms while claiming one.

**What a shared packet costs when the rooms are not identical.** Put the
plug of PULPO into B and leave A open. The packets are still shared —
they must be, the encoder never saw a room — but four `approach` rows
now disagree, and the body has no way to ask which room it is in. That
is DynamicAlias: same WSP, different dynamics. It is measured here and
reported as a number (`dynamic_alias_with_hole`), and it is **not**
fixed: writing the room into ext.domain would break I2, and writing it
into ext.seq would put 324 places under a 256 ceiling and destroy the
sharing this slice exists to demonstrate. The hole belongs to ROOM-2.

No portal: a door whose packet is local-only *is* an alias in that cell,
so it would smuggle in ROOM-2's problem. A→B is a teleport, as in
WORLD-3.

SELF-1 — "was that me, or was that the floor?"

PULPO-C changed strategy because a curriculum taught the body the cube it
was standing in. That is adaptation, not attribution: the body was told
nothing about *why* its predictions went wrong, and it did not need to
know. Here it does.

Two perturbations, and the observation they produce is the same sentence:
`approach` did not land where T said it would.

    motor   the body slips. `approach` pushes along DIRS[(h + slip) % 6]
            while the heading of the pose does not turn. The cube, the
            floor, the goal and the start are untouched.
    world   one corridor voxel turns to stone. The motor is intact.

Neither perturbation is announced. Nothing is written into the WSP, into
`kind`, into `extract` or into E: the packet for a pose is byte-identical
in both arms, and there is no CONCIENCIA atom, no second CAM and no
fourth action. The only new state is one integer:

    body_offset in 0..5     "my approach pushes along (h + body_offset)"

Six hypotheses, all integers. The body can state them because it already
owns the ring: "push along (h + k)" is exactly "what `avoid` k times then
`approach` used to do", and T learned both before anything moved. So the
hypothesis is written in the body's own actions, never in coordinates.

What the self-model buys is not speed, it is **not rewriting the world**.
On a surprise the plain agent updates T at once: that is right when the
floor moved and wrong when the arm did. SELF-1 holds the update, counts
which of the six hypotheses would explain the errors it is holding, and
only then decides — commit them (the world changed) or drop the ones the
body explains (it was me). A tie is not me: it commits.

SENSOR-1S evaluator: private truth against what the consumer received.

Two independent sources judge everything. The tap's raw log holds every
message as Gazebo delivered it, written before the injector or the adapter
can touch it. The host transcript holds every header the consumer was
sent and the hash of the bytes that actually crossed. The adapter's own
send log is only compared with the transcript, never walked. The
consumer's tally is recomputed from the transcript and must match.

Every transcript record is matched to exactly one raw capture by (source,
capture time, payload hash); every raw capture the injector did not remove
must be delivered exactly once; every header field that is not a
measurement is pinned; every delivery time is bounded below by when the
tap received the message and when the injector released it. Floats are
lab measurements, never agent state.

CORTEX-1 — the turn where the slow clock changes a decision.

Two cells. The first one carries a **sign**, in Spanish, and the sign is
the only thing that separates the two layouts:

    prize   SIGN: "AMBAR: entra. El siguiente sitio es el premio."
    trap    SIGN: "AMBAR: no entres. El siguiente sitio es una trampa."

SIGN is index 0 and KIND_EMPTY in both, so `encode_cell` produces the
**same 16 bytes** in both worlds. The fast loop sees that packet, a flat
Q row and an empty T, and it has no way whatever to tell prize from trap:
it does not read Spanish, and nothing in WSP carries the sentence. Greedy,
a flat row is `wait`, so the fast agent stands still in both.

The cortex reads the record (which carries the extract, i.e. the sign),
answers in atoms, and `loop._propose` hands that answer to the gate. In
prize it proposes UNIR → approach → +16. In trap it proposes TEMER →
avoid → 0 instead of walking into −16.

What is *not* claimed: the sign is not verified. `has_fact` on that slot
means "a sign was there", never "the sign told the truth" — the world put
the string there, the same way the ring puts `cell=11 kind=NOVEL` there.
The cortex writes nothing: no CAM, no T, no Q. It proposes; the gate
decides; the world pays.

The KPI turn is turn 0, greedy, on a fresh agent. Nothing is trained
first — training would give Q an opinion, and the point is precisely a
decision Q cannot have an opinion about.

    PYTHONPATH=. python3 -m echoai.nexus0.sign

SIGN-C — the turn where being wrong is what makes the slow clock speak.

WORLD-3 already showed that T survives a change of topology and is wrong
in exactly one place: the fork. CORTEX-1 already showed that a sentence
the fast loop cannot read can change a decision. Neither of those is this
slice. This one is the join: **the contradiction is the reason**.

    train in HOME      T learns the spine, Q learns the last three nodes
    walk into SHIFT    same CAM, same T, same Q, one edge moved
    stand on the fork  Q says approach with margin >= ESC_MARGIN,
                       T says the successor is C, and the world has
                       posted a sign here in Spanish
    act                the world hands back the other node
    only now           the slow clock is woken, with REASON_CONFLICT and
                       with the origin's own sentence, and its atom is
                       consumed on the next turn

The order is the claim. Nothing reads the sign before the world has
contradicted the map: `_conflict_origin` merely copies it, and
`cortex.complete` is not reached until after `env.step()`. A slice that
consulted the sign first would be CORTEX-1 with a longer walk-up.

What the fast loop is *not* short of: the ordinary ATTEND ladder is on in
the `ladder` arm below, wakes on the landing node for LOW_C, reads that
node's own record, and earns nothing. Same cable, same stub, same world.
Only the reason differs, and only the conflict reason carries the
sentence from the place where the commitment was made.

Two things measured here came out against the plan, and both are in the
report as numbers rather than as prose:

**1. At a hazard the fast loop needs no cortex.** The intended landing
node was WORLD-3's X, a THREAT, on the reasoning that a flat Q row waits
and collects nothing while `avoid` pays +8. It does not: `loop.turn`
hands a threat cell `E[U] = 80`, `U_SHORT` is 60, and `gate`'s second
MODIFY rule turns that proposed `wait` into `avoid` before the world sees
it. The fast arm collects the +8 by itself and the ROI of any cortex that
proposes `TEMER` there is exactly 0. `placements()` prices both landing
kinds and prints the number; the bench uses the one that can come out
differently, because a control that cannot lose is the experiment run
twice.

**2. TEMER cannot earn in this world at all.** The only two positive
payoffs are `approach` at a GOAL (+16) and `avoid` at a THREAT (+8), and
the gate already takes the second one for free. So the sign says what the
world actually changed — the lever reversed, what was the hazard is now
the prize — and the atom that follows from it is `UNIR`. The verb is one
of the three this bench has; no fourth action, no new reward, no new
edge. The successor table is `graph.NEXT[shift]` imported verbatim; the
single byte SIGN-C owns is the *kind* of the node the moved edge lands
on, and that node is unreachable in HOME either way.

    PYTHONPATH=. python3 -m echoai.nexus0.signc

SIM-3 — declarative worlds, real physics, and an information boundary.

This package is infrastructure, not cognition. Nothing here imports the
fast loop, WSP, CAM, Q or the gate, and nothing here is allowed to hand
simulator truth to the process that receives ticks. See
``echoai/docs/SIM3-DESIGN.md`` for the contract this implements.

Floats live here because SDF and Gazebo are float physics. They stop at
the boundary: every quantity SIM-3 itself reasons about (poses, sizes,
grids, tolerances) is an exact integer in millimetres.

``python3 -m echoai.nexus0.sim3`` — validate, preflight, bench, audit.

Every command prints JSON to stdout and returns a non-zero exit code when
the thing it checked did not close. A missing dependency prints its cause
and the next command to run; it never prints a number it did not measure.

Private side of SIM-3: the only process that talks to Gazebo.

Runs inside the pinned container, never on the host, and never in the
same process as the consumer. It speaks one JSON line per message over
stdin/stdout to the supervisor. Everything it reports — sim time, rig
pose, model poses, contacts — is read back out of the running backend's
entity component manager or off a sensor topic. Nothing here reads the
manifest, the split, the seed or the roles: it is handed an effective
SDF and a model name and that is all it knows.

Stdlib plus the Gazebo Python bindings only; it is mounted read-only and
its bytes are hashed into the run record.

Mutant backend: a Gazebo that runs but reports a clock that never moves.

Used only by the mutant group, and named in the run label. The bench must
notice that the observed sim time stopped advancing and go red with
``clock_not_monotonic`` — a supervisor that trusted the step counter and
synthesised times would sail past this.

The SIM-3 consumer: an instrumental probe, deliberately adversarial.

It is not an agent. It has no policy, no memory and no cognition; it
answers ticks and it tries, on every run, to reach everything it must
not be able to reach. Two channels and no more:

* stdin/stdout is the tick socket — one JSON line in, one ACK out;
* stderr is a one-way report to the evaluator.

The report says what the probe could see, verbatim. It does **not** say
whether that was allowed, and it is not told what the canaries are — if
it knew the secret it was hunting for, finding it would prove nothing.
The evaluator, which does know, decides.

Stdlib only. Runs under bubblewrap with a cleared environment, a fresh
network, PID, IPC, UTS and cgroup namespace, and a mount namespace that
contains a read-only /usr, this file, and an empty /work.

A consumer that misbehaves on purpose. Never part of the 24 bench runs.

The tick channel is supposed to be inert: an ACK is an acknowledgement,
not a command, and nothing a consumer writes back should reach Gazebo.
This probe tries anyway — extra fields, an oversized body, a wrong
sequence, a service call shaped like an entity spawn — and the
supervisor is expected to record a violation and close the session.

Its sessions are labelled ``adversarial_transport`` in the report so that
a reader never mistakes them for bench evidence.

An auditor that does not read ``sim3_green``.

It rebuilds the evidence instead: it regenerates the twelve rehearsal
packages from the published seeds, re-hashes every trace file, recomputes
the fall, the resting height, the contact and the tick count from the raw
frames, and recomputes the protocol commitment and the code inventory.
Only then does it compare its own numbers with what the report claims.

``evidence_valid`` means the evidence reconstructs. It does not mean the
bench passed: a red report with perfectly reconstructible traces is
exactly what an honest failure looks like.

``--self-test`` mutates copies of the report — a flipped result, a bumped
counter, a rewritten trace hash, two different runtime locks — and
requires each to be rejected. Detection is claimed only from a positive
control that the auditor accepted first.

before any of this ran. A group is ``pass``, ``fail`` or ``not_run``;
a missing dependency is never ``pass``, and ``sim3_green`` requires
every mandatory group in ``pass`` plus the existing NEXUS-0 regression.

The bench writes one trace file per Gazebo run and records its hash, so
the auditor can recompute every number here from the traces instead of
believing the summary. It also writes red results: a failing case keeps
its measurement and its cause.

Fast, honest SIM-3 CI entry point.

Unit validation always runs. A backend bank is requested only with
``SIM3_CI_BACKEND=1``; if unavailable its machine-readable status remains

These documents are reviewed inputs to an experiment. They are never mounted
into the consumer sandbox and none of their fields are observations.

The evaluator. It sees the truth; it never answers back.

Everything here reads private data — the manifest, the roles, the rig
poses, the canaries — and turns it into a verdict. Nothing it computes
is written to the tick channel; the only direction of travel is towards
the report.

Two things it deliberately does not do:

* it does not soften a criterion. The numbers come from the frozen
  protocol, and a run that misses one is red with its measurement
  attached;
* it does not accept the probe's word for whether an access was allowed.
  The probe reports what happened; this module decides what that meant,
  and it is the only side that knows the canaries.

A declarative world generator with a PRNG you can reimplement.

Two rules shape this module.

*The generator may build connectivity; it may not hand over its
solution.* The flood fill decides whether a candidate is admissible and
then the path is discarded. Nothing about it reaches the manifest, the
report or the consumer.

*Reproducible means reproducible in another language.* Python's
``random`` is a Mersenne Twister whose stream is an implementation
detail; SplitMix64 is nine lines of integer arithmetic, so an auditor
can regenerate seed 7 without running our code. Bounded draws use
rejection, not modulo, so the distribution is exactly uniform.

Rejected candidates consume an index and are written to a ledger. A
world the generator could not close is a number in the report, never a
quietly reduced difficulty.

Millimetre integers, and the exact-decimal gate that produces them.

SDF is written in metres as decimal text. The profile only admits values
that land exactly on a millimetre, so parsing is a decimal operation, not
a float one: ``0.1`` becomes ``100`` because ``Decimal("0.1") * 1000`` is
``100``, never ``100.00000000000000005``. Anything that does not land on
a millimetre is refused rather than rounded, because rounding here would
silently move a wall.

Everything downstream — AABBs, the free-space grid, the fingerprint, the
tolerances — is integer millimetres.

Metamorphic pairs: two questions with known answers.

*Rename and reorder.* The same geometry written with the model names
permuted and the XML in a different order must produce the same
fingerprint, the same physics and — the part that matters — a tick
transcript the consumer cannot tell apart. If a name changed anything
visible, the boundary would be leaking identity.

*Move a wall.* Shifting one barrier by 500 mm must change the private
AABBs, change what the backend's entities report, and change what the
rig collides with — while the consumer's transcript stays identical. A
hash that changes while the simulator behaves the same would mean the
world file is decorative.

Every transformed package is validated again from scratch before it is
run, exactly like a fresh one.

Mutants: every refusal must be provoked from a control that passed.

The rule SIM3-DESIGN.md §6 insists on is easy to violate by accident:
checking that an already-red report is still red proves nothing. So each
mutant here starts from a *positive control* — a package, a session or a
seal that has just been verified to work — applies exactly one defect,
and requires the failure to name that defect. A mutant that fails for the
wrong reason is recorded as a failure of the mutant, not as a success.

Packages: hash first, structure second, geometry last.

A SIM-3 package is two files and nothing else. Validation is deliberately
ordered:

1. the bytes are hashed and compared with the manifest **before** any
   parser sees them, so a manifest can never describe a file other than
   the one that runs;
2. JSON Schema checks shape;
3. this module checks everything JSON Schema cannot say — that roles
   form a bijection with the models, that the spawn is not inside a
   wall, that the floor actually holds the rig up, and that the station's
   approach point is reachable through the inflated geometry.

The flood fill is a private evaluator artefact. It exists so the bench
can refuse an impossible world; it is never exported, and the consumer
never learns that it ran.

The trusted rig, and the systems the supervisor is allowed to add.

A world in SIM-3 is data: it cannot ask for code. Systems come from the
fixed, versioned list below and are written into a *copy* of the world —
the effective SDF — which is hashed separately from the source. Confusing
the two hashes would let a world be certified by one file and run as
another, so both travel through the report side by side.

The rig itself is a sphere of known radius and mass with a contact
sensor. It is inserted from here, identically in every world, at the
private spawn column. It is instrumentation: it is not an agent, it is
not controlled, and dropping it proves gravity and collision — nothing
about aerodynamics.

One host runner for ``preflight → bench → audit``.

It builds the pinned local image only when it is absent. It never pulls a
different image, and it refuses to overwrite a changed runtime lock without
an explicit acknowledgement. That makes a host/runtime change visible before
it can become an apparently comparable report.

Preflight: find the real tools, or say plainly that they are missing.

``runtime-lock.json`` is the answer to "what actually ran". It records
the host, the container image digest, the exact Debian package versions
of gz-sim, libsdformat and gz-transport inside it, the Python that drove
them, the sandbox binary and the hashes of every file of ours that took
part. ``latest`` appears nowhere and no Fuel asset is fetched.

A missing dependency produces ``available=false`` and a reason. It never
produces a substitute: SIM-3 would rather publish ``not_run`` than a
number a mock invented.

The consumer's cage, and the one wire that leaves it.

The isolation here is a mount/network/PID namespace built by bubblewrap,
not a Python object that declines to expose an attribute. The consumer
gets a read-only /usr, an empty tmpfs working directory, its own copy of
/proc, and this file. It does not get the repository, ``lab/``, the
package, the suite, the supervisor's environment or argv, a network
namespace with a route, or any sibling process to look at.

Two file descriptors carry everything: stdin/stdout is a preopened
socketpair (the tick channel), stderr is a one-way report to the
evaluator. There is no third.

This closes accidental leaks and direct access by the probe. It is not a
claim about kernel escapes or timing side channels, and the report says
so. If bubblewrap is absent or the kernel refuses the namespaces, the
isolation group is ``not_run`` — a mocked permission is not a permission.

The ``sim3-boxes-v1`` SDF profile: a closed grammar, not a filter.

Two properties matter more than convenience here.

*Closed*: anything the profile does not name is refused. Not ignored, not
stripped — refused, with a cause. An SDF that smuggles a ``<plugin>`` or
an ``<include>`` past a lenient reader would let a world choose its own
code, and the whole point of SIM-3 is that the world is data.

*Exact*: geometry is read as decimal millimetres (see ``geom.mm``), so
the AABB this module returns is the same integer on every machine, and a
hash over it means something.

libsdformat is consulted as well (see ``runtime.check_sdf``), because a
file this module accepts must also be a file Gazebo accepts. Neither
check substitutes for the other: ours is stricter, theirs is the truth
about what the backend will load.

Commitments, derived seeds, and an exam you can only open once.

Three separate mechanisms, deliberately not merged:

* **commitment to the protocol** — publish ``SHA256(tag || protocol
  digest || secret)`` before anything is generated, so the rules cannot
  be rewritten afterwards;
* **seed derivation** — ``HMAC-SHA256(secret, tag || split || index)``,
  so seeds are reproducible by the custodian and unguessable by anyone
  else;
* **inventory commitment plus a sealed→opened→consumed latch** — so a C
  partition is opened exactly once, by one process, and stays consumed
  even if that process dies mid-run.

SIM-3 exercises all three with a **rehearsal** secret that is published
on purpose (32 bytes of ``0x01``). A hash alone is not custody: the
custodian and the access log live outside this file, and outside this
repository.

One episode: Gazebo on the private side, a probe on the public side.

The supervisor is the only place the two ever meet, and the only thing
that crosses is a clock. A tick is literally three fields:

    {"v":1,"seq":<n>,"sim_time_ns":<observed>}

``sim_time_ns`` is read out of the running backend. If Gazebo does not
start, or stops advancing, there is no tick to send: the supervisor has
no code path that manufactures one. That is the whole point of putting
the stepping behind a request/response instead of a timer.

Everything else the run produces — poses, model entities, contacts,
package identity, split, seed — stays on the private side and goes to
the evaluator, never back down the socket.

SLEEP-2: consolidate repeated CAM/T transitions into compact rules.

The source of a rule is the existing memory pair: CAM supplies the WSP state
and ``World`` supplies observed transitions and their counts.  Consolidation
runs off the fast path, reads both, and writes only a bounded rule table.  It
does not delete, relabel or rewrite a CAM slot or a T row, and it never calls
the cortex.

A rule is structural rather than positional:

    (WSP with seq removed, action) -> (next WSP template, seq delta)

It survives only when at least ``MIN_ORIGINS`` distinct T rows support one
uncontradicted result.  One heavily repeated location is therefore not a
general rule.  Prediction restores the local seq into the same 16-byte WSP.

STREAM-1: long external WSP streams with DynamicAlias measured.

An external producer supplies a transition as ``(wsp, action, next_wsp)``.
Frame sequence and chunk identifiers remain outside that interface.  They are
useful to audit a long stream, but they must not become a hidden state id in
the 16-byte packet or in CAM/T.

The processor reuses the Agent's existing CAM allocator and ``World`` table;
it neither chooses actions nor creates a second predictor.  DynamicAlias is
reported when one equal ``(wsp, action)`` pair has multiple observed next
packets.  The correct response in this slice is to measure it, never to hide
the chunk in domain, style or seq.

TALK-1 — posthumous subtitles. Never a thought, never a cause.

This file reads `thought.jsonl` and writes Spanish. That is all it does,
and the order of those two things is the whole claim: the turn already
happened, the animal already decided, the world already paid. What is
produced here is a **subtitle**, in the cinema sense — it arrives after
the scene and changes nothing in it.

So there is no import of `Agent`, of the loop, of CAM, of T, of Q, of the
gate, of the cortex or of any world; no `parse_reply`, no `NAVI_CORTEX_*`,
no network, no subprocess, no server. The file is opened read-only and its
bytes are the same afterwards. Nothing here is a callback, a pipe or a
file the animal reads back. Standard library only.

**No `porque`.** The log records what happened, not why. `attend_on` says
the slow clock woke; `action` says what the body did after the gate;
`cortex_action` says which proposal was spent this turn. Those are three
facts and this module prints them as three clauses. Joining them with a
conjunction would be inventing the one thing the record does not contain.
Even on the turn that spends a proposal the two stay apart, because
`gate_decision` still has the last word — that is the same separation
SIGN-Cc had to be fixed to make.

The output is controlled Spanish, not prose: a closed set of sixteen
labelled clauses, one line per record, in the order the records came in.
Each clause maps to exactly one field, and `Q` and `WSP` are reproduced
verbatim rather than interpreted. An auditor can therefore check the
subtitle against the record without ever calling `render`.

    python3 -m echoai.nexus0.talk echoai/lab/thought.jsonl

A malformed record is an error and a non-zero exit, never a default and
never a skipped line. The whole file is validated before a single subtitle
is emitted, so there is no such thing as half a narration that reads as a
whole one.

A future Qwen pass that polishes these lines into nicer Spanish would be
another **optional operator** consuming subtitles that were already
audited. It is not implemented here and must never be part of `green()`.

TALK-1 bench — does the subtitle say what the record says, and nothing else?

`talk.py` writes the Spanish. This file never calls it to check itself: an
auditor that asked the renderer what the renderer meant would score a
tautology. Instead `audit()` parses the subtitle back into its sixteen
labelled clauses and checks each one against the record with rules written
here, independently — including the rules that say what a clause must
**not** contain, which no renderer can satisfy by accident.

Three things are measured and all three are numbers, not flags:

    TranslationConsistency   clauses that survive the audit, over a matrix
                             that floods every field the log has
    mutants_killed           hand-corrupted subtitles that must be caught
    causal_writes            findings of an AST scan over `talk.py` itself

The matrix is generated from field values, not recognised by turn or cell:
the meaning has to come out of the record. Two of its rows are not
synthetic at all — the real `conflict` / `consume` pair SIGN-Cb produced,
and a real OPEN-1 turn where the body opened a jar — because a bench that
only ever narrates records it wrote itself has not met the animal.

    PYTHONPATH=. python3 -m echoai.nexus0.talk1

`cortex.jsonl` only holds the ~40 turns that woke the slow clock. This
is the other log: the whole run, including the quiet turns, so the ring
can be replayed and watched. Fixed keys, integers and atoms, no field
for prose — same contract discipline as `cortex_turn.py`.

It is a record of what the fast loop did. It is not a brain render.
Dev tools for nexus0. Not imported by the fast loop.

CI never imports this as a requirement. Tests cover should_speak() and

A 4B model is not the claim. The claim is the *cable*: something outside
the fast loop reads the language the world put in front of it and answers
in atoms, and the loop treats that answer as a proposal the gate can still
refuse. This file is that something, in twenty lines, so CI never needs a

is no sign it says nothing at all, and the loop must fall back to Q and
count a reject. Saying nothing is a real answer here — a cortex that
always speaks is a cortex that cannot be wrong.

Contract: docs/ECHO45-EGO-MEMORIA1-DESIGN.md (approved, 2026-09-25).

World (simulated agents; the lying is programmed, no person is deceived):
  each episode ECHO must find a key hidden in one of 6 places. It asks one of 5 agents for a hint.
  Liars give a wrong place most of the time. Walking to a place costs 3 turns; checking a hint
  first costs 1. Working memory is wiped after every episode: only what ECHO WRITES survives, and
  writing an entry costs 1 turn. Nobody tells ECHO what or when to write.
  In a world with debts, agents later CLAIM payment for an old episode ("I gave you the right
  place in episode 12, you owe me"). Honest agents claim only what is true; liars also claim for
  episodes where they lied. ECHO can reject a false claim only by citing its diary entry (hash);
  otherwise it pays (6 turns).
ECHO (integers only):
  valence of an entry = turns saved (+) or lost (-) because of that hint;
  trust(agent) = sum of valences of the entries about it (so the diary CAUSES whom it trusts);
  Q_write[context][write|skip] and Q_check[trust sign][check|go] learned from the delta they caused.
Every run is deterministic from its seed; every entry is hash-chained.
